patterns: which data structure should i use
entries.answer: A data structure is a particular way of arranging data in memory so that some operations become cheap and others become expensive, and choosing one is usually the decision that determines whether an algorithm is fast enough. The trade is between lookup, insertion, deletion and memory, and no structure wins all four: an array gives fast indexed access and slow middle insertion, a hash table gives fast lookup and no order at all, a tree gives ordered data with logarithmic cost, and a graph models connections at the price of expensive traversal. The structure also determines the data type in a typed language, since a stack and a queue are often built-in types rather than something you write yourself. What matters in practice is matching the structure to the dominant operation rather than to the data, because a structure chosen for reads in a write-heavy program is a poor trade even though its lookup time is excellent.

entries.answer: A stack is a collection that only lets you add and remove at one end, the top, which makes it last in first out: the most recent item added is the first one you get back. That single restriction is the whole design, and it is what makes a stack the right model for anything where the most recent thing matters most, such as undo history, the call stack that tracks which function called which, the browser back button, and matching brackets in a parser. Adding is push and removing is pop, both constant time, and the related peek returns the top without removing it. The mistake people make is reaching for a stack when they actually need a queue, since both look like a list of pending work and produce a completely different order of processing. A stack that grows without bound is also the mechanism behind a stack overflow, when a recursive function calls itself before the base case returns.

entries.answer: A queue is a collection where items are added at one end and removed from the other, which makes it first in first out: the first item that arrived is the first one served. That ordering is the point, and it is what a queue is for, so the right questions are about fairness and about what happens when the items being handled take different amounts of time. Breadth first search is the textbook example, because exploring a graph level by level and choosing a queue is what keeps it from wandering into a single deep branch. In a real server a queue also buffers a burst of arriving work so that a service processing one request at a time is not overwhelmed when a thousand arrive at once. The two known variations are a circular queue, which reuses the array positions freed at the front, and a priority queue, which ignores arrival order and serves the highest priority item first, which is implemented with a heap rather than a plain array.

patterns: what is a doubly linked list
entries.answer: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node stores a value and the address of the next node, rather than a single contiguous block of memory like an array. That layout is the whole trade: inserting or deleting at a known position is constant time because you just relink the neighbours, but finding the element at position n is linear because you have to walk the chain, and there is no random access. It also allocates one small block per node, which costs more memory and more cache misses than an array, so the array is faster in practice for almost every ordinary program. The variants exist to serve different access patterns: a singly linked list points one way, a doubly linked list adds a backward pointer so traversal runs both directions, and a circular list links the last node back to the first. The structure still matters in a language without a built-in dynamic array, and it is the right choice for a work queue where removal from the front is frequent.

entries.answer: A hash table stores key and value pairs and looks an entry up in roughly constant time by running the key through a hash function that turns it into an index into an array of buckets. If two keys land in the same bucket that is a collision, and it is resolved either by chaining, where each bucket holds a list, or by open addressing, where the algorithm probes for the next free slot. The average case is fast, and the whole subject of database index design is how to keep it that way, because the table degrades sharply when every key hashes to the same bucket. A load factor above roughly 0.7 makes collisions common enough to matter, so implementations grow the table and rehash everything when the ratio passes a threshold. The interface is simple, the ordering is not, so iterating a hash table gives no useful order, and any algorithm that needs sorted output has to sort the keys separately.
